## Setting Up the Problem (Bayes' Theorem)

**Given:**
- Prevalence: P(D) = 1/500 = 0.002, so P(no D) = 0.998
- Sensitivity: P(+|D) = 0.98
- Specificity: P(–|no D) = 0.95, so P(+|no D) = 0.05 (false positive rate)

**Applying Bayes' Theorem:**

$$P(D|+) = \frac{P(+|D)\,P(D)}{P(+|D)\,P(D) + P(+|\text{no }D)\,P(\text{no }D)}$$

**Numerator:**
P(+|D)·P(D) = 0.98 × 0.002 = 0.00196

**Denominator terms:**
- True positives: 0.00196
- False positives: P(+|no D)·P(no D) = 0.05 × 0.998 = 0.04990

Total P(+) = 0.00196 + 0.04990 = 0.05186

**Posterior probability:**

$$P(D|+) = \frac{0.00196}{0.05186} = 0.037794...$$

Converting to a percentage: **3.7794%**

## Sanity Check

This result illustrates the classic base-rate effect: even with a fairly good test (98% sensitivity, 95% specificity), because the condition is rare (0.2% prevalence), the pool of false positives (≈49.9 per 1000 people) vastly outnumbers the pool of true positives (≈1.96 per 1000 people). So among all positive tests, only a small fraction are true cases — about 1 in 26.
